**Title: The Willow and the Lantern**

In the eleventh year of the reign of Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang Dynasty, in the mist-laced province of Jiangnan, there stood a quiet village nestled beside a winding black river known as the *Yin Shui*, or the "Veiled Stream." The river wound through ancient willows, their long, weeping branches touching the water like fingers tracing secrets. The villagers spoke little of the stream after dusk, for it was said that ghosts walked its banks, drawn by grief or unfinished vows.

There was one story they told only when the moon was veiled by clouds.

It began with a young scholar named **Liu Jian**, son of a minor magistrate, who had returned from Chang’an after failing the imperial examinations for the second time. Heartbroken and weary, he sought solace in his ancestral village by the Yin Shui. There, he was drawn to a secluded pavilion beneath a great willow tree where, legend whispered, a maiden had once drowned herself in sorrow.

Her name was **Mei Ling**. Fifty winters past, she had been betrothed to a young poet from the capital. But he never returned from war. Grief-stricken, and pressured by her family to marry another, Mei Ling slipped away one autumn night and flung herself into the Veiled Stream. Since then, the villagers had seen a pale figure beneath the willow, always holding a single paper lantern, its flame cold and blue.

Liu Jian was a man of reason—scholars scoffed at ghosts. Still, on the seventh night after his arrival, he found himself drawn to the pavilion. The air was thick with the scent of wet earth and plum blossoms. The moon cast fractured light through the willow’s tresses. As he sat by the water, he saw a soft glow approaching—*a lantern*, floating without a hand to hold it, its flame a flicker of icy blue.

Then she appeared.

Mei Ling stood at the water’s edge, her hair unbound and streaming like riverweed, her robes of old silk, water-stained and spectral. But her face—her face was as alive as any living woman’s, except for her eyes, which held no reflection.

“You do not fear me, scholar,” she said, her voice like wind through reeds.

“I am a servant of reason,” Liu Jian replied, though his heart hammered like a war drum.

“You are curious,” she whispered, stepping closer. “Like *him*.”

“Him?”

“The poet who promised to return.”

She told her story—how he had carved her name into the willow’s bark with his knife, how he’d sworn to come back and write poems beneath this very tree. But his letters ceased. She waited a year. Then two. She drowned not from sorrow, she said, but from betrayal—until she learned years later, as a spirit, that he had died at the pass of Qilian, clutching a scroll of love poems meant for her.

“He never betrayed me,” she said. “But I betrayed myself. Now I wait—not for him, but for one who will carry his words back to the world.”

Liu Jian, moved, took out his inkstone. “Tell me the poems.”

So she recited—verses of moonlight and plum blossoms, verses of longing so deep they made the water tremble. He wrote them down under the weeping willow, his brush moving as if guided by unseen hands. As he copied the final line, the lantern's flame turned from blue to golden.

“I have waited fifty years,” Mei Ling breathed. “But you… you have a scholar’s heart.”

Then the wind stilled. The lantern sank into the water and vanished.

When Liu Jian awoke at dawn, his scrolls were filled with verses no historian had ever recorded—the lost poems of Wei Yan, the forgotten poet of the western frontier. He wept as he read them, for they were exquisite.

He journeyed back to Chang’an with the poems bound in silk. When the Imperial Academy read them, they hailed Wei Yan as a lost master of the age. His name was restored. His legacy reborn.

But Liu Jian never spoke of the willow, the river, or the woman of mist.

Years passed. He became a high scholar, beloved and wise. Yet every autumn, on the night of the ninth moon, he would return to the village by the Yin Shui. He would sit beneath the willow, now deeply carved with names—both his and Mei Ling’s—and light a single paper lantern. He would set it upon the stream and whisper:

> *“The words live. You are remembered.”*

And sometimes—just sometimes—villagers claimed to see two lanterns drifting side by side: one golden, one pale blue, floating downstream into the mist, like two souls finally at peace.

But others said that on still nights, if you stand beneath the weeping willow with a heart unburdened by disbelief, you can still hear the soft rustle of silk… and the faint, melancholic melody of a poem no living man has ever learned.
